label: Claude Opus 5.5
output:
Dear Nana,

Hi Nana. I wish it was me sitting at that table and not a piece of paper, but Denise has promised to read this properly and not rush through the good parts. Denise, if you're skipping ahead, she can tell. She always could.

First, I'm sorry I'm not there. I know you've already told me it's fine. Mom's told me, Denise has told me, and I've half told myself. But I still feel bad about it, so I'm saying it once and then I'm done. I'm on call all week and I couldn't find anyone to take it. And before you ask: no, nothing has broken yet. I'll let you know.

I've been trying to write this for about a week. Every time I sat down I'd get two sentences in, get all choked up, and shut the laptop like it had done something to me. So if this comes out a bit all over the place, that's why. I made myself finish it this time because I didn't want you to leave that kitchen without hearing some of this.

Fifty-one years on Kathleen Street. I've been trying to get my head around that. You were in that house before the maple out front was much of anything, before Mom and Denise were grown, and long before me. Half this family was raised in that kitchen. Maybe more than half. Everybody I love has sat at that table at some point, eating something you made and getting told to sit up straight.

I know everyone's going to go on about the house this week, so here's my part.

When I think of that house, I mostly think of summers. Staying up way too late watching the Expos, and later the Jays, on that little TV on the counter, because you'd made me a deal: I could stay up as long as I dried the dishes. I think I dried more dishes in those summers than I have in my whole adult life since. I'm pretty sure you were running extra dishes through the sink just to keep the game going, and I never once called you on it.

I think of the back steps at six in the morning. You'd be out there with your tea and I'd come out in my pyjamas and sit beside you, and you wouldn't say a single word until the cup was empty. Not one. It took me years to realize that wasn't you being grumpy. That was just how you started the day, and you let me be part of it. I still don't really talk to anyone before my first coffee. People at work think it's a personality thing. It's not. It's yours.

And I think about crib. You taught me when I was about seven, and you never once let me win. Not when I was little, not on my birthday, not when I was sulking. You'd peg out and say "good game" like you meant it, and I'd go stomp around the yard. Then when I was fifteen I finally skunked you. I've never seen you look so proud and so annoyed at the same time. And you went and made me a whole pan of butter tarts, which I think tells you everything about how you love people. You make them earn it and then you feed them.

Honestly, I don't think I've ever been prouder of anything than that game. I have a job now where I keep big computer systems running for a lot of people, and when it goes well that's a nice feeling, but it's not skunking-Nana-at-fifteen good. Nothing is.

Speaking of my job. When I moved to Toronto you mailed me a twenty-dollar bill taped inside a card that said "for pizza, you look thin on the computer." I still have the card. I spent the twenty on pizza, because you told me to and I'm not stupid. I've told that story to probably fifty people, and every one of them wishes you were their grandmother. You can't have them. You're mine.

And then last Christmas, when my pager went off in the middle of dinner and I had to get up from the table, you asked me if the internet was broken again and if I'd fixed it. Now you ask me that every single time we talk. "Did anything break?" I want you to know that's my favourite part of every call. Some weeks it's the only time anyone asks me that and actually cares what I say. So keep asking. And for the record, most of the time I did fix it.

Okay. Here's what I really wanted to say, and Denise, take your time with this part.

I'm proud of you, Nana. Really proud. You looked at all of this and decided for yourself that it was time. Nobody pushed you and nobody made the choice for you. You went and looked at places and picked Elmwood Terrace because you liked it. I know that couldn't have been easy, leaving a house you've lived in for fifty-one years, the house you and Grandpa Walt made into what it is. I don't think I'd have the guts. But you've always been the toughest person in this family, and the most sensible, and you're doing it the same way you do everything: on your terms, with your mind made up, and probably with a list.

I know Grandpa would be proud of you too. I think he'd be telling everybody at Elmwood about you by the end of the first week.

I don't want this to sound like a funeral, because it isn't one. The house was never really the walls or the cupboards. It was you in it. You're the one who made the tea and dried the dishes (okay, made me dry the dishes) and raised all those kids and kept the crib board out on the table. All of that's coming with you. The kitchen on Kathleen Street was great, but I think it was great because you were in it, and I'm pretty sure Elmwood is about to find that out.

And I've done my research, Nana. Elmwood has a crib league. A real one. I think somebody should warn them. Those people have no idea what's about to move onto the second floor. I'd give it a month before you're running it. Please be gentle with them, at least for the first week. Then do whatever you want.

I hear your room looks out at the parking lot and a big maple. Do me a favour and look at the maple and not the parking lot. You can have your tea by that window in the morning and not talk to anybody until the cup's done, and anybody who interrupts you can deal with you.

And you've still got your Tuesday crib with the church ladies. Don't let them think they're getting rid of you that easily.

A few house things I know you're worrying about. Denise is taking the cuckoo clock and the cedar chest, so those are staying in the family and will be well looked after. She has also promised me she'll keep the clock wound, and if she doesn't, I'll hear about it from you. I asked for the crib board. I hope that's okay. I couldn't imagine anything else from the house I'd want more. I'll take good care of it, and I'll keep using it, which is the point.

That brings me to the most important part of this letter.

I'm coming up the weekend of December 5th, as soon as my rotation's done. Nobody's pager is coming with me. I'm bringing the crib board, and you and me are going to sit down at your new place and play the first game there. I'll tell you everything that broke, and you can tell me all about the new people and which ones you've already beaten.

I'm warning you now, I've been practicing. I'm not saying I'm going to skunk you. I'm just saying you might want to start thinking about butter tarts.

I love you so much, Nana. Thank you for the kitchen, and the summers, and the back steps, and the twenty dollars, and for never once letting me win. Enjoy your last night on Kathleen Street. Then go show Elmwood Terrace how it's done.

See you December 5th. Bring your A game.

All my love,
Aidan

P.S. Denise, you can stop reading now. Go give her a hug from me.
